newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: CASH CALLS SUGGEST HEALTHIER S.AFRICA STOCK MARKET.
newsitem.headline: CASH CALLS SUGGEST HEALTHIER S.AFRICA STOCK MARKET.

text.p: Recent moves by some of South Africa's biggest firms to tap investors for cash have been hailed as another sign of renewed confidence in its nervous markets, but analysts on Friday warned that progress may not be steady.
Thursday saw three companies announce plans to raise cash to fund ambitious expansion schemes.
"The fact that they are prepared to go ahead shows that they must have done some homework to convince them sentiment will be positive," said Denzil Newman, portfolio maanger at Syfrets.
Drinks giant South African Breweries Ltd opened the show by saying it was considering an issue of up to 2.0 billion rand worth of new shares.

Just hours later, Anglo American Industrial Corp Ltd (Amic) announced a rights issue to reap 1.2 billion rand and investment group NSA Investments Ltd said it wanted to net 280 million rand from the market.
The flood of schemes came two days after chemicals group AECI Ltd announced plans to unbundle its Afex Holdings Ltd investment that include a placing of 12 percent of the firm.
News of the big deals saw share prices retreat modestly on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange on Friday, reflecting concerns the moves could squeeze billions of rand out of the spot market.
But the cash calls have added to a feeling that, seven months after the rand began its spectacular descent, stability has finally returned to South Africa's battered markets.
"We have broken the bear market scenario," said David Shapiro, a managing director at stockbroker Frankel Pollak.
Recent record gains on Wall Street and other top financial markets have also helped spur South African sentiment.

The share issues are expected to be generously discounted to ensure their success and attract foreign investors still concerned about putting their money in South Africa. But the market sees the cash calls as easily succeeding.
"Confidence is returning, share prices are going up and the rights issues will be well received. There is plenty of money sloshing about," said one share dealer, who declined to be named.

Sentiment has been boosted by a rand that has stabilised against the U.S. dollar and sterling, and encouraging economic data. August consumer inflation, announced on Thursday, rose from 7.1 percent in July, but came in lower than expected at 7.5 percent.
However, analysts said talk of a return to a booming market with foreign cash pouring into the country was premature.

Old worries over political and economic stability and South Africa's spiralling violent crime rate still deterred foreigners. "We have turned a corner, but it is going to be marked by fits and starts," Newman said.
Scares over the rand or political crises are still likely to occasionally rock the market in the coming months. "Another bout of rand weakness would spook the market," he said.
The one thing that is most likely to tempt massive foreign investment back to South African markets is a rapid move towards privatisation -- a central plank of the government's macro-economic plan.
South Africa's telecomunications giant Telkom is earmarked as the first major project with more to follow.
Adam Jacobs, economic trends analyst at ABSA bank, said he didn't expect any concrete progress before next year, but that once privatisation gets under way overseas investors could well pile in.
"Until we get privatisation moving things will be subdued. But from then on, it may be a different story," he said.
